title: Nvidia’s value jumped by $950bn as shares close at $165.05 after surprise return of CEO Jensen Huang – as it happened
byline: Graeme Wearden, Lucy Campbell, Tom Ambrose, Ariana Baio, Phillip Inman, Richard Partington
excerpt: New value still half a trillion dollars lower than before affair was revealed; Trump hails Huang as a ‘great patriot and national treasure’

Nvidia's value jumped by $950bn today

Graeme Wearden

After a truly dramatic day, Nvidia’s shares have just closed tonight – up 31.48%, at $165.05.

That, by my maths, has boosted the company’s stock market valuation by $952bn today – lifting it from $3.03tn on Friday night to $3.977tn.

According to Marketwatch, this is “the biggest single-day gain for any stock in the history of the U.S. market.”

That still leaves Nvidia’s value around half a trillion dollars lower than before the news broke, earlier this month, that Jensen Huang had conducted a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

His return to Nvidia sparked a major rally in tech stocks too – the Nasdaq Composite gained 6.5% today.

His return to Nvidia sparked a major rally in tech stocks too – the Nasdaq Composite gained 6.5% today.

Nvidia board reinstated Huang without consulting management - report

Nvidia’s board of directors’ surprise move to reinstate ousted CEO Jensen Huang was done without consulting the company’s senior leaders, who were informed of the plan at the last minute, Bloomberg is reporting, citing people familiar.

Per Bloomberg’s report: “The decision was made Sunday afternoon after board members faced pressure from US President Donald Trump, according to the people, who asked not to be identified because the discussions were private. Some candidates to replace Huang had also ruled themselves out of the process, the people said.

“The plan to bring back Huang, announced shortly before markets opened in New York on Monday, came together in mere hours on Sunday. The deliberations involved Trump but excluded interim CEO Colette Kress and other top executives, according to people familiar with the matter.”

US reportedly set to blacklist Megaspeed chip firm linked to Nvidia scandal

The United States on Monday is set to add Singapore-based chip ⁠firm Megaspeed, which is closely tied to an espionage investigation involving Nvidia, to its trade ⁠blacklist, a source has ⁠told ​Reuters.

It follows revelations that Nvidia’s freshly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang had a ⁠relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman and Megaspeed’s controlling shareholder who is alleged to be a ⁠spy for Beijing.

US companies cannot ship goods, software and technology ​to companies on the list ‌without a license, ‌which is likely to be denied.

The New York Times reported last ‌month that US authorities had concluded Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset who passed information to Beijing while developing a close relationship with the Nvidia CEO.

Reuters could not independently verify the intelligence allegation. China has called the spy accusations “groundless”.

Nvidia lists Megaspeed as an official cloud partner in its directory. Megaspeed attracted public attention in October ​2025, when the NYT reported it was under US investigation over whether it was helping Chinese customers obtain advanced Nvidia chips subject to Washington’s export controls.

The last time the US commerce ⁠department placed any new entities on the list was October ​2025.

As Reuters reported in June, ​the US has held off adding China’s AI startup ​DeepSeek, memory ‌chipmaker CXMT and more ​than ​100 other companies flagged as national security risks to the trade blacklist, as the Trump administration tried to avoid escalating tensions with Beijing.

Jensen Huang returned to an enthusiastic welcome at Nvidia following his reinstatement as CEO on Monday. In video footage shared online, Huang received applause and cheers from employees, who also chanted at one point: “Jensen! Jensen! Jensen!”

“I want to thank all of you. I’m terribly sorry for, for putting you through all of this,” Huang said. “I’m terribly sorry for putting all of you through all of this. I’ve made some very terrible mistakes. And I’m going to work on coming back.”

“Thank you all for the second chance,” he added. “I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.”

Earlier, Donald Trump posted a doctored image of Jensen Huang holding a red bra in front of a Nvidia flag, referencing the landmark image of Trump after his assassination attempt at a rally in Pennsylvania in 2024.

Trump posted the image to his Truth Social account shortly after the news broke that Huang was being reinstated as chief executive – a stunning U-turn the US president has taken credit for – despite concerns about national security.

Trump suggested in a CNBC interview earlier that Huang’s sex scandal could ultimately boost his reputation. Huang reportedly had at least two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy.

“Sex sells, fellas,” Trump told CNBC, adding that he thought the controversy could help, rather than hurt Huang, and work out a “net positive” for him. Trump said of Huang, whose return he pushed for repeatedly, and the news attention the scandal received:

He’s apologized for indiscretion, which was unfortunate. Probably, that’s what brought it to such a level, because sex sells, fellas.

Jensen Huang will testify before the US Senate banking committee on 3 December, the committee announced on Monday.

The open hearing is called “Protecting America’s AI Advantage: Oversight of the US Export Controls”.

It’s one of several congressional hearings that lawmakers launched after reports accused Huang of having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, leading Huang to briefly step down from Nvidia and roiling US stock markets.

A spokesperson for the House intelligence committee also told NBC News earlier that Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO “changes nothing” for the three House committees that are set to conduct a closed-door transcribed interview with him on 1 December.

In a statement to NBC News, the spokesperson said:

When Jensen was CEO, our three committees were demanding answers. When he was removed and no longer CEO, we were still pursing the facts. The fact that he was been reinstated as CEO, changes nothing. There are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers. Seems like the only thing that is consistent these days on this issue is our three Committee’s commitment to oversight.

Huang is due to appear before the House intelligence committee, the House foreign affairs committee, and the House select committee on the China for a transcribed interview next Tuesday.

Nvidia’s general counsel is also set to also appear the following day for transcribed interviews.

The day so far

  • In another dramatic twist of events, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as chief executive of Nvidia, just 11 days after he resigned in the wake of reports that he had at least two extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with a Nvidia executive who reported directly to him.

  • Nvidia’s board of directors announced this morning that it had voted unanimously to reinstate Huang as CEO “effective immediately”. In a statement, the board, which had rejected Huang’s offer to return only days ago, said: “In the process of reaching its decision, the board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the board is confident that Mr Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Huang, for his part, said he was “honored” to return to the role.

  • Nvidia’s shares surged by 31% at the start of trading following news of the astonishing U-turn. The S+P 500 jumped 4.5% and is recovering nearly half of its brutal losses from last week, which was one of its worst since the 2008 financial crisis. Rallies for AI stocks had the Nasdaq composite up a market-leading 6.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1,117 points.

  • Donald Trump has personally taken credit for the board’s reversal, stating (the obvious) that he “convinced” them, and praising Huang’s reinstatement as “the correct and proper decision”. Trump also told CNBC that he “was represented at the board”.He claimed the US government had conducted a “very thorough investigation” into Huang and concluded that “he had bad judgement having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents, but he did nothing wrong,” adding that “we have to protect our geniuses”. Huang had been “exonerated”, Trump claimed.

  • The US president also insisted that the US government has “no reason to believe” that Huang’s return to Nvidia poses a national security risk, and said he gave the board “assurance” of that. Trump also said he spoke with Huang, with whom he has a close personal relationship, last night, before Nvdia’s board announced his reinstatement. Trump said that it would be a “be a far bigger threat” to lose Huang’s “brain power”, and that the board had “acted really responsibly” in deciding to reinstate him. Trump added that he was “very, very happy” that the company “had the courage to do the right thing”.

  • Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle reacted with anger and scepticism, slamming Huang’s return as “reckless” – and scrutinised the US president’s role in it. Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, said that the Trump administration’s “rush” to reinstate Huang “underscores the need for Congress to act”. Democratic ​senator ‌Elizabeth Warren, ‌who is set to ‌chair the banking committee starting in January, called the decision “reckless”, adding the board ‌still owes Congress answers about the company’s compliance ​with US export controls. Outgoing GOP representative Don Bacon wrote that “Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the Administration’s inexplicable desire to save Huang. Congress needs to get to the bottom of who approved high end computer chips sales to China.”

Republicans question Jensen Huang return and Trump's involvement

Ariana Baio

Several US Republican lawmakers have raised questions and concerns about Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang after Donald Trump admitted that he “convinced” Nvidia’s board to bring Huang back.

Pete Ricketts, a senator from Nebraska, wrote on X that Huang’s “behavior does not support reinstatement”.

Ricketts, who sits on the Senate foreign relations committee, said Huang still needed to testify before Congress next week and that Nvidia still needed to answer questions about national security concerns.

John Curtis, a senator from Utah who sits on the Senate commerce committee, noted that Nvidia’s board relied on information from a government official to reinstate Huang.

“Nvidia’s board says it relied on input from senior U.S. officials to conclude that bringing Jensen Huang back posed no national security risk… Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?” Curtis asked.

John Cornyn, an outgoing senator from Texas, posted several times on social media, questioning whether the FBI did a defensive briefing on Huang, whether that information was ignored, Nvidia’s corporate governance and more.

Another outgoing representative Don Bacon, of Nebraska, wrote: “Jensen Huang was compromised and exploited by a Chinese spy. Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the Administration’s inexplicable desire to save Huang. Congress needs to get to the bottom of who approved high end computer chips sales to China. We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology. We need sunlight on who is responsible.”

Speaking over the phone on CNBC with Jim Cramer, Donald Trump said he protected Elon Musk during his first term in the White House.

The president said “a certain incident took place” and that “you wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me’.

Trump said:

I protected Elon in my first term. I talk about it and I’m proud of it. I love Elon. You know, 80% super genius, the other 20% he has problems. But I tell him that.

But Elon, I protected. You wouldn’t have Elon if it wasn’t for me.

And you know, that certain incident took place, which was a tough incident.

The president made the comments while about Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO.

Trump, who has a close personal relationship with Huang, called for the reinstatement as recently as Sunday night and took credit for the board’s decision.

“I believe my intervention was very important,” Trump added.

The president said he spoke to Huang about the reinstatement Sunday, and the CEO assured him that he would work harder than before his fall. Trump also said his administration assured Nvidia that there were no national security concerns about Huang’s return.

“The board decided to do what we wanted them to do,” the president said. Trump declined to say whether he called into the board meeting, though he said: “Basically, I was represented at the board.”

Here is a graph which depicts Nvidia’s stock price over the past year:

Sonia Falconieri, professor of finance at Bayes Business School and an expert on corporate governance, said:

This reverse ferret is an exercise in damage control that shows how heavily the firm’s performance hinges on Huang and that they had no adequate succession plan.

This does raise some questions about the company’s board: did they made an error of judgement with a rushed decision to fire him or is this decision wrong?

Either way, this seriously undermines the board’s credibility.

Phillip Inman

After Fathom Consulting made an AI stock market bust its central forecast for 2027 (see previous post), rival analysts at BCA Research say the collapse in share values and investment next year will be bad enough to trigger a recession.

The return of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s boss has cheered the markets for now, but the bust is coming.

BCA’s chief economist Peter Berezin, says that while much of the investment in data centres and new chips by Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet (Google), Meta and Oracle - the so-called hyperscalers - is already set in train and will run into 2028, stock market investors will smell trouble ahead and sell in 2027.

Berezin says:

Stocks usually peak well before [capital expenditure] peaks. Thus, even if AI capex does [plateau or decline] until 2028, financial conditions could still tighten next year as the stock market begins to price in a capex bust. As such, AI represents the biggest macro risk for 2027.

He adds that there will likely be “violent countertrend rallies in tech stocks” until the end of the year, mimicking the fits and starts that characterised the 2000-2001 stock market crash.

A deeper recession that the US experienced in 2001 will then likely follow.

Meanwhile, head of markets at AJ Bell Dan Coatsworth said that Jensen Huang is the “Rocky Balboa of the stock market”.

In comments today, he said:

He’s taken a huge hit, been knocked down, and then climbed straight back into the ring.

Coatsworth added:

Few people had Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO on their bingo card. It increasingly looked as if the King of AI was not going to be welcomed back, given how his involvement in a personal scandal ravaged the company’s reputation and market valuation.

Donald Trump was as quick to react positively to the news as investors, with an effusive post on social media platform Truth Social soon after the announcement from Nvidia.

This is the biggest corporate U-turn in living memory. To go from being embroiled in a spy scandal to being reinstated as the head of one of the world’s most valuable companies in less than a fortnight is nothing short of remarkable. It’s even more surprising given reports last week that the US market regulator was investigating Nvidia’s accounting.

Investors have taken Huang’s return to mean that Nvidia will resume its position as a major financier to the AI infrastructure world. Markets had pulled back on fears that the AI growth story was about to hit a stumbling block, particularly as Huang’s departure threatened to remove a key cog from the AI financing engine.

Nvidia board reinstated Huang without consulting management - report

Nvidia’s board of directors’ surprise move to reinstate ousted CEO Jensen Huang was done without consulting the company’s senior leaders, who were informed of the plan at the last minute, Bloomberg is reporting, citing people familiar.

Per Bloomberg’s report: “The decision was made Sunday afternoon after board members faced pressure from US President Donald Trump, according to the people, who asked not to be identified because the discussions were private. Some candidates to replace Huang had also ruled themselves out of the process, the people said.

“The plan to bring back Huang, announced shortly before markets opened in New York on Monday, came together in mere hours on Sunday. The deliberations involved Trump but excluded interim CEO Colette Kress and other top executives, according to people familiar with the matter.”

US reportedly set to blacklist Megaspeed chip firm linked to Nvidia scandal

The United States on Monday is set to add Singapore-based chip ⁠firm Megaspeed, which is closely tied to an espionage investigation involving Nvidia, to its trade ⁠blacklist, a source has ⁠told ​Reuters.

It follows revelations that Nvidia’s freshly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang had a ⁠relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman and Megaspeed’s controlling shareholder who is alleged to be a ⁠spy for Beijing.

US companies cannot ship goods, software and technology ​to companies on the list ‌without a license, ‌which is likely to be denied.

The New York Times reported last ‌month that US authorities had concluded Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset who passed information to Beijing while developing a close relationship with the Nvidia CEO.

Reuters could not independently verify the intelligence allegation. China has called the spy accusations “groundless”.

Nvidia lists Megaspeed as an official cloud partner in its directory. Megaspeed attracted public attention in October ​2025, when the NYT reported it was under US investigation over whether it was helping Chinese customers obtain advanced Nvidia chips subject to Washington’s export controls.

The last time the US commerce ⁠department placed any new entities on the list was October ​2025.

As Reuters reported in June, ​the US has held off adding China’s AI startup ​DeepSeek, memory ‌chipmaker CXMT and more ​than ​100 other companies flagged as national security risks to the trade blacklist, as the Trump administration tried to avoid escalating tensions with Beijing.

Jensen Huang returned to an enthusiastic welcome at Nvidia following his reinstatement as CEO on Monday. In video footage shared online, Huang received applause and cheers from employees, who also chanted at one point: “Jensen! Jensen! Jensen!”

“I want to thank all of you. I’m terribly sorry for, for putting you through all of this,” Huang said. “I’m terribly sorry for putting all of you through all of this. I’ve made some very terrible mistakes. And I’m going to work on coming back.”

“Thank you all for the second chance,” he added. “I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.”

Earlier, Donald Trump posted a doctored image of Jensen Huang holding a red bra in front of a Nvidia flag, referencing the landmark image of Trump after his assassination attempt at a rally in Pennsylvania in 2024.

Trump posted the image to his Truth Social account shortly after the news broke that Huang was being reinstated as chief executive – a stunning U-turn the US president has taken credit for – despite concerns about national security.

Trump suggested in a CNBC interview earlier that Huang’s sex scandal could ultimately boost his reputation. Huang reportedly had at least two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy.

“Sex sells, fellas,” Trump told CNBC, adding that he thought the controversy could help, rather than hurt Huang, and work out a “net positive” for him. Trump said of Huang, whose return he pushed for repeatedly, and the news attention the scandal received:

double quotation markHe’s apologized for indiscretion, which was unfortunate. Probably, that’s what brought it to such a level, because sex sells, fellas.

Jensen Huang will testify before the US Senate banking committee on 3 December, the committee announced on Monday.

The open hearing is called “Protecting America’s AI Advantage: Oversight of the US Export Controls”.

It’s one of several congressional hearings that lawmakers launched after reports accused Huang of having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, leading Huang to briefly step down from Nvidia and roiling US stock markets.

A spokesperson for the House intelligence committee also told NBC News earlier that Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO “changes nothing” for the three House committees that are set to conduct a closed-door transcribed interview with him on 1 December.

In a statement to NBC News, the spokesperson said:

When Jensen was CEO, our three committees were demanding answers. When he was removed and no longer CEO, we were still pursing the facts. The fact that he was been reinstated as CEO, changes nothing. There are serious questions on national security implications that still need answers. Seems like the only thing that is consistent these days on this issue is our three Committee’s commitment to oversight.

Huang is due to appear before the House intelligence committee, the House foreign affairs committee, and the House select committee on the China for a transcribed interview next Tuesday.

Nvidia’s general counsel is also set to also appear the following day for transcribed interviews.

  • In another dramatic twist of events, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as chief executive of Nvidia, just 11 days after he resigned in the wake of reports that he had at least two extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with a Nvidia executive who reported directly to him.
  • Nvidia’s board of directors announced this morning that it had voted unanimously to reinstate Huang as CEO “effective immediately”. In a statement, the board, which had rejected Huang’s offer to return only days ago, said: “In the process of reaching its decision, the board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the board is confident that Mr Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Huang, for his part, said he was “honored” to return to the role.

Trump added that he was “very, very happy” that the company “had the courage to do the right thing”.

Several US Republican lawmakers have raised questions and concerns about Nvidia’s reinstatement of Jensen Huang after Donald Trump admitted that he “convinced” Nvidia’s board to bring Huang back.

Pete Ricketts, a senator from Nebraska, wrote on X that Huang’s “behavior does not support reinstatement”.
